goal: Kilby is running a museum, a working farm, a cafe, and a campground, and it is doing it with one marketing day a week. That context makes the results more impressive: a single post announcing the new breakfast reached about 70,000 people organically, the Facebook following is 5,200, the Google rating is 4.6 stars across 433 reviews, Tourism Harrison partnerships bring in new followers, and locals are returning for the cafe and the rotating workshops. The campground books itself, so the work in this plan is not about filling it. The gap is everything that sits between a person discovering Kilby and a person walking through the door. The WordPress site has been built by many hands over many years, with 257 images on the homepage, a 67 out of 100 speed score, and no clear path to the museum, the cafe, or the campground. There are no Reels on Instagram, engagement sits at 0.3 percent, outdated third-party pages show the wrong information in search, and booking is manual and heavy on admin time. The next ninety days are designed around your calendar. You are open to the public for a few more weeks, so the first two weeks capture content while the animals, the store, and the cafe are in front of you. Then the break begins, and that quiet season is the best time to rebuild the website and write the content that makes AI tools and search engines describe Kilby accurately. By the February campground announcement, which gets your highest email open rate, everything points to a faster and clearer site. The three results you named are the ones this plan is built to move: steady website traffic growth, more social followers, and stronger reach among locals. Every week is sized to fit one day.
